# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

	wpcom_remote_login_remove_dom_node_classes( "wpcom_remote_login_msg" );
	wpcom_remote_login_remove_dom_node_id( "wpcom_remote_login_key" );

// Watch for messages back from the remote login
window.addEventListener( "message", function( e ) {
	if ( e.origin === "https://r-login.wordpress.com" ) {
		var data = {};
		try {
			data = JSON.parse( e.data );
		} catch( e ) {
			wpcom_remote_login_final_cleanup();
			return;
		}

		if ( data.msg === 'LOGIN' ) {
			// Clean up the login check iframe
			wpcom_remote_login_remove_dom_node_id( "wpcom_remote_login_key" );

			var id_regex = new RegExp( /^[0-9]+$/ );
			var token_regex = new RegExp( /^.*|.*|.*$/ );
			if (
				token_regex.test( data.token )
				&& id_regex.test( data.wpcomid )
			) {
				// We have everything we need to ask for a login
				var script = document.createElement( "script" );
				script.setAttribute( "id", "wpcom_remote_login_validate" );

					+ '&wpcomid=' + data.wpcomid

					+ '&host=' + window.location.protocol
					+ '//' + window.location.hostname
					+ '&postid=6856'

				document.body.appendChild( script );
			}

			return;
		}

		// Safari ITP, not logged in, so redirect
		if ( data.msg === 'LOGIN-REDIRECT' ) {
			window.location = 'https://wordpress.com/log-in?redirect_to=' + window.location.href;
			return;
		}

		// Safari ITP, storage access failed, remove the request
		if ( data.msg === 'LOGIN-REMOVE' ) {
			var css_zap = 'html { -webkit-transition: margin-top 1s; transition: margin-top 1s; } /* 9001 */ html { margin-top: 0 !important; } * html body { margin-top: 0 !important; } @media screen and ( max-width: 782px ) { html { margin-top: 0 !important; } * html body { margin-top: 0 !important; } }';

			return;

		// Safari ITP
		if ( data.msg === 'REQUEST_ACCESS' ) {
			console.log( 'request access: safari' );

			// Check ITP iframe enable/disable knob
			if ( wpcom_remote_login_extra_auth !== 'safari_itp_iframe' ) {
				return;
			}

			// If we are in a "private window" there is no ITP.
			var private_window = false;
			try {
				var opendb = window.openDatabase( null, null, null, null );
			} catch( e ) {
				private_window = true;
			}

			if ( private_window ) {
				console.log( 'private window' );
				return;
			}

			var iframe = document.createElement( 'iframe' );
			iframe.id = 'wpcom_request_access_iframe';
			iframe.setAttribute( 'scrolling', 'no' );
			iframe.setAttribute( 'sandbox', 'allow-storage-access-by-user-activation allow-scripts allow-same-origin allow-top-navigation-by-user-activation' );
			iframe.src = 'https://r-login.wordpress.com/remote-login.php?wpcom_remote_login=request_access&origin=' + encodeURIComponent( data.origin ) + '&wpcomid=' + encodeURIComponent( data.wpcomid );

			var css = 'html { -webkit-transition: margin-top 1s; transition: margin-top 1s; } /* 9001 */ html { margin-top: 46px !important; } * html body { margin-top: 46px !important; } @media screen and ( max-width: 660px ) { html { margin-top: 71px !important; } * html body { margin-top: 71px !important; } #wpcom_request_access_iframe { display: block; height: 71px !important; } } #wpcom_request_access_iframe { border: 0px; height: 46px; position: fixed; top: 0; left: 0; width: 100%; min-width: 100%; z-index: 99999; background: #23282d; } ';

			style.type = 'text/css';
			style.id = 'wpcom_request_access_styles';
			style.appendChild( document.createTextNode( css ) );
			document.body.appendChild( style );

			document.body.appendChild( iframe );
		}

		if ( data.msg === 'DONE' ) {
			wpcom_remote_login_final_cleanup();
		}

NGA transfers Homeland Security Infrastructure Program to DHS

  • Home

 June 9, 2022

 Media Relations
 mediarelations@nga.mil
 (571) 557-5450

 press-releases, dhs, department-of-homeland-security, data

SPRINGFIELD, Virginia – The National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency is transitioning responsibility for the Homeland Security Infrastructure Program to the Department of Homeland Security. 

The HSIP is also known as the Homeland Infrastructure Foundational Level Data, or HIFLD, program. NGA will no longer directly provide HIFLD data content or services through its digital platforms. NGA will also remove legacy HIFLD services across all NGA domains. 

To reach HIFLD support and current data content, NGA customers and mission partners should use the DHS GMO’s unclassified online, on-demand data delivery services at HIFLD open (https://hifld-geoplatform.opendata.arcgis.com ) and HIFLD secure (https://gii.dhs.gov/hifld/data/secure ). Please submit HIFLD questions or concerns to the HIFLD inbox (HIFLD@hq.dhs.gov). 

HIFLD is a compilation of more than 455 data layers that cover national critical infrastructure for the U.S. and U.S territories. Since 2002, NGA has sponsored and provided oversight for HIFLD to procure, review and deliver HIFLD data layers in support of the homeland security and homeland defense mission. The data layers support preparedness and readiness, response and recovery decision making at the state, local and national levels, and event/incident response mapping to include recent efforts for the California wildfires, and Hurricanes Harvey, Irma and Maria. A few notable mission partners include FEMA, NORAD-NORTHCOM, the National Interagency Fire Center, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers and the U.S. Department of Transportation. 

“This transition shall ensure program efficiencies are gained by centralizing HIFLD data procurement, creation, and dissemination; eliminate potential competing and disconnected NGA and DHS program planning cycles and allow for more successful coordination and collaboration with State and local HS/HD mission partners,” said Rexford Tugwell, NGA’s Office of Geography.

For questions or concerns regarding the transition of HIFLD responsibility, please contact the NGA HSIP transition team, NGAHSIPTransitionTeam@nga.mil.

#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Homeland Infrastructure Foundation-Level Data (HIFLD) Open
Organization/publisher: Department of Homeland Security
Description: The public-facing portal for the HIFLD program, providing geospatial data and tools for planners, analysts, and others throughout the homeland security enterprise, supporting missions including law enforcement, border protection, emergency management, critical infrastructure protection, and national operations and data fusion centers.
URL: https://www.dhs.gov/gmo/hifld

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

Let me fetch the DHS page and the atcoordinates post.# HIFLD Open: Research Report

## Summary

The most important finding is that **HIFLD Open no longer exists as a federal resource.** DHS shut the public portal down on **August 26, 2025**. The HIFLD website and portal were fully removed by **September 16, 2025**. The DHS program behind it continues, but only for authorized users. Copies of the public data now survive in non-federal archives (Section 7).

---

## 1. Checking your information

| Field | Your info | What I found |
|---|---|---|
| **Title** | Homeland Infrastructure Foundation-Level Data (HIFLD) Open | ✅ Correct. Note that HIFLD Open was a *portal holding a collection* of roughly 270–455 separate geospatial layers (the count changed over time). It was not a single dataset. |
| **Publisher** | Department of Homeland Security | ✅ Correct but broad. More precisely: DHS Management Directorate → Office of the Chief Information Officer (OCIO) → **Geospatial Management Office (GMO)**, led by the DHS Geospatial Information Officer. Before that, the **National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency (NGA)** sponsored the underlying program from 2002 until its formal transfer to DHS in 2022. Most layers were *created* by other agencies (USGS, FEMA, NOAA, EPA, USACE, Census, Oak Ridge National Laboratory and others). HIFLD collected and republished them. |
| **Description** | "The public-facing portal for the HIFLD program… law enforcement, border protection, emergency management…" | ⚠️ Partly right. That mission list describes the **HIFLD program as a whole**, which DHS says serves the "homeland security enterprise" (HSE). HIFLD Open's own tagline was narrower and aimed at the public: *"National foundation-level geospatial data within the open public domain that can be useful to support community preparedness, resiliency, research, and more."* |
| **URL** | https://www.dhs.gov/gmo/hifld | ⚠️ This is the DHS **program page**. It now describes HIFLD Secure and the discontinuation (last updated 09/04/2025). The actual Open portal was **hifld-geoplatform.opendata.arcgis.com**, later hifld-geoplatform.hub.arcgis.com. It ran on Esri ArcGIS Hub through GeoPlatform.gov and is offline. |
| **Status** | (implied active) | ❌ **Discontinued August 26, 2025.** |

---

## 2. Who published it, and how the program was organized

- **Current owner:** DHS GMO, within OCIO. Contact: **HIFLD@hq.dhs.gov**.
- **The HIFLD program now has these parts:**
  - **HIFLD Open** (public domain, public access). Decommissioned.
  - **HIFLD Secure** (formerly HSIP Gold). Commercially licensed and For Official Use Only (FOUO) data, hosted on the DHS Geospatial Information Infrastructure (GII). Access requires a GII account (non-DHS users need a DHS-authorized Login.gov account), a MyHIFLD profile and an approved Data Use Agreement. It is limited to users supporting homeland security or homeland defense missions.
  - **"HIFLD Shared" and the "HIFLD Catalog"** appear in DHS's 2026 HIFLD User Forum videos. The Catalog is described as a way for organizations to share authoritative datasets with the HSE. I couldn't find public documentation of HIFLD Shared's access rules.
- **Partners:** GMO runs HIFLD with agencies that rely on the data. It collects use cases from across the HSE to decide which datasets to buy or renew. It also holds an annual user forum for HIFLD Secure users.
- **Data producers:** Many federal agencies, Oak Ridge National Laboratory (which produced many of the layers) and commercial vendors.
- **Former governance body:** The FGDC HIFLD Subcommittee, created in February 2002. Members were OASD(HD&ASA) at DoD, the DHS office now known as CISA (then NPPD Office of Infrastructure Protection), NGA, and the USGS National Geospatial Program. The subcommittee was **retired in March 2026**. FGDC says the DHS GMO program "meet[s] or exceed[s] the original intent of the subcommittee."

---

## 3. Legal authority

**Main statute:** 6 U.S.C. § 343(b), which is Homeland Security Act § 703 as amended by **Intelligence Reform and Terrorism Prevention Act of 2004 (P.L. 108-458), § 8201**. It:
- creates the Office of Geospatial Management within DHS OCIO, run by a Geospatial Information Officer;
- directs the CIO to run a program for the "efficient use of geospatial information," including "providing such geospatial information as may be necessary to implement the critical infrastructure protection programs" and meeting the needs of those responsible for "planning, prevention, mitigation, assessment and response to emergencies";
- requires coordination with the FGDC and compliance with **OMB Circular A-16** and **Executive Order 12906**, plus standards set under **E-Government Act § 216**.

Congress's findings in § 8201 said DHS's geospatial preparedness was "insufficient" because of poor data compatibility, insufficient data sharing, and technology barriers.

**Internal policy:** DHS Management Directive 034-01 (Geospatial Management) formally creates GMO, which DHS dates to 2004.

**What the law does not do:** As far as I can tell, no statute requires a *public* portal. The law requires DHS to provide geospatial information for critical-infrastructure and emergency missions, not to the general public. That is why DHS could end HIFLD Open while keeping HIFLD Secure. DHS's stated reason was that the public portal was "no longer a national mission priority."

**Related frameworks (context only):** The Geospatial Data Act of 2018, the OPEN Government Data Act (part of the Evidence Act of 2018), and federal critical-infrastructure policy (PPD-21 and its 2024 successor, NSM-22). I did not confirm any explicit HIFLD Open provisions in these, so treat them as background.

---

## 4. History

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| Nov 1, 2001 | A post-9/11 meeting in Norfolk, VA starts the effort. It began as a planned "Common Relevant Operating Picture" (Bill Dollins, *geoMusings*, who was in the room). The group was briefly called "FGDWG," and early prototypes ran on Esri ArcIMS. |
| Feb 2002 | HIFLD Working Group/Subcommittee formed. NGA begins sponsoring the **Homeland Security Infrastructure Program (HSIP)** and its data packages (HSIP Gold, restricted; HSIP Freedom, releasable). |
| 2004 | IRTPA § 8201 creates the DHS geospatial office (now GMO). |
| Feb 2015 | NGA leadership orders HSIP support ended by the end of FY15. In March, DHS, NAPSG and NSGIC write memos opposing this. NGA and DHS agree instead to move HSIP to DHS by the end of FY18. |
| Feb 2016 | **HIFLD Open launches** on GeoPlatform/ArcGIS Open Data with 270+ public-domain datasets from HSIP 2015. Some were re-hosted copies; others were live links to the source agency's service. The "HSIP" name is retired in favor of "HIFLD." |
| 2017 | Temporary "HIFLD4Harvey" and "HIFLD4Irma" portals (the latter also used for Maria) serve 12,850 users in about 30 days. |
| 2018 | HIFLD wins the FGDC Doug D. Nebert Award. The portal had 300+ products, 35,472 users and 31,695 downloads since launch. |
| Jun 9, 2022 | NGA formally announces the HSIP/HIFLD transfer to DHS (455+ layers). NGA removes its legacy HIFLD services. |
| ~Mar 2025 | DHS announces it will end HIFLD Open and keep HIFLD Secure (date per an August 2026 FGDC/NGAC presentation). |
| Jun 24, 2025 | NAPSG Foundation publishes the notice. Initial target: by Sept 30, 2025. Layers hosted only on Open would move to Secure; some would be available from the original providers. |
| Aug 2025 | The shutdown date moves up to **Aug 26, 2025**. DHS publishes a "crosswalk" spreadsheet linking each layer to its original source. |
| Sep 2025 | HIFLD website and portal removed (Sept 16). The crosswalk also goes offline. NAPSG and GMO survey users to set HIFLD Secure priorities. |
| Nov–Dec 2025 | Volunteer archives completed (Section 7). |
| Mar 2026 | **HIFLD Next** launches. FGDC HIFLD Subcommittee retired. |
| 2026 | DHS's HIFLD User Forum covers the discontinuation, HIFLD Shared and Secure, and the new HIFLD Catalog. |

---

## 5. What the data contained

- **About 400+ national layers at shutdown.** The Data Rescue Project archived 415.
- **Coverage:** The U.S. and its territories. Topics included energy (power plants, substations, transmission lines, pipelines, refineries), communications (cell towers, antenna structures), transportation (airports, ports, rail), water (treatment plants, reservoirs), public health (hospitals, nursing homes, child care centers), education (schools), emergency services (fire, EMS, law enforcement, emergency operations centers), government facilities, flood hazard products, natural hazards (seismic, volcanic, tsunami), administrative boundaries (e.g., 119th Congressional districts), and hydrography.
- **Formats:** CSV, KML/KMZ, shapefile, file geodatabase, GeoJSON, and ArcGIS REST feature services and APIs.
- **License:** Mostly public domain, but DHS warned that "some HIFLD data may be subject to copyright restrictions." Terms were listed per layer, so check each one.
- **Citation format DHS used:** "U.S. Department of Homeland Security. HIFLD. HIFLD – Homeland Infrastructure Foundation-Level Data. [Year]. [Access date]. https://hifld-geoplatform.hub.arcgis.com/."

---

## 6. Users and public benefits

**Users:**
- FEMA, NORAD-NORTHCOM, the National Interagency Fire Center, USACE and USDOT (NGA's list of "notable mission partners")
- State and local emergency managers. For example, New Orleans used HIFLD for emergency response and large events, and Oregon OEM built its own crosswalk catalog after the shutdown.
- Fusion centers and law enforcement
- Utilities setting power-restoration priorities for hospitals and nursing homes
- University researchers studying cascading failures, climate vulnerability and environmental justice
- Rural counties with little GIS staff
- Civic tech groups, journalists and Esri Living Atlas

**Benefits:**
- **One place for national data.** Users didn't have to gather and standardize data from dozens of agencies themselves, the "M: drive problem" HIFLD was created to solve.
- **Disaster response.** Used for Hurricanes Harvey, Irma and Maria, and for California wildfires including the 2018 Camp Fire.
- **Fairness of access.** Small governments and the public had the same baseline data as federal agencies.
- **Reproducible research.** Studies could cite one stable, well-known source.

---

## 7. Preservation status (most useful for archivists)

| Copy | Who holds it | Details |
|---|---|---|
| **DataLumos (ICPSR)** | Data Rescue Project, coordinated by Frank Donnelly, Brown University Library | 415 layers, one record each, with original titles, descriptions and keywords. Formats: file geodatabase, GeoJSON, GeoPackage, shapefile. Includes an index plus the **DHS crosswalk**: "HIFLD OPEN GIS Data Index and Crosswalk," DOI **10.3886/E241367V1**. Completed Dec 2025. |
| Bulk download | Brown University Library | Globus transfer (instructions on Brown's Data Rescue GitHub) and a DRP bulk torrent of about 170 GB. |
| **Source Cooperative** | SeerAI, Inc. (source.coop/seerai/hifld) | Most layers converted to spatially sorted Parquet, with an inventory CSV. Released under CC BY 4.0. Nov–Dec 2025. |
| **HIFLD Next** | Public Environmental Data Partners and Fulton Ring (hifld.publicenvirodata.org) | Launched March 2026 from the DRP archive. GeoParquet, PMTiles, GeoJSON, shapefile and file geodatabase. Map and table previews, version history, JSON API, open-source code (AGPL-3.0). A "HIFLD Next Commons" coalition is forming to maintain it, possibly with OpenStreetMap US, building on Project Geospatial's "Phoenix Project" proposal. |
| NASA NCCS mirror | NASA Center for Climate Simulation | Selected layers from May 2019 (older). |
| Agency sources | Original producers (via the crosswalk) | These provide current versions, where they still exist. |

**Gaps and cautions:**
- One small civic-tech site (My Community Data) reported in March 2026 that only about **52 of roughly 365** former HIFLD service URLs still worked. It said communications (0 of 13), flood products (0 of 31) and energy (2 of 43) were hit hardest. I couldn't independently verify this audit.
- The archives are **frozen snapshots from August 2025**. A hospital that opened later won't appear, and a closed facility will still be listed. Donnelly expects the archive to be current enough for "the next couple of years," then mainly historical.
- Some layers moved only to HIFLD Secure, so there is **no current public version** of them.
- Counts differ by source (270, 300+, 400+, 415, 455, ~495). This reflects the date of each count and whether Secure layers were included.
- Possible remaining tasks: capture Wayback Machine copies of the portal and item pages, and keep original item IDs (needed to match layers to the crosswalk).

---

## 8. Notes for data scientists

- Each layer is different: different source agencies, update schedules, fields and accuracy. Always check the layer's own metadata.
- Known quality problems, per HIFLD Next: outdated records, bad geocoding (e.g., points at 0,0 "null island"), and missing useful attributes such as hospital bed counts.
- The original ArcGIS REST root (services1.arcgis.com/Hp6G80Pky0om7QvQ) and the hub URLs should be treated as dead. Old scripts and apps that called them will fail.
- Cloud-friendly formats (GeoParquet, PMTiles) are now available through Source Cooperative and HIFLD Next.

---

## 9. Policy issues

- **Transparency vs. security.** HIFLD grew out of 9/11 security concerns, and the split between Open and Secure always reflected that tension. Ending Open gave authorized government partners data the public no longer has.
- **Thin justification.** DHS said only that the portal was no longer a mission priority. It gave no cost figures or security reasons.
- **The crosswalk replacement was criticized** for making every user collect data from many sites again (Project Geospatial called it "a regression"). The crosswalk itself was taken offline in September 2025.
- **Fragility of single federal portals.** This case is now discussed as an example in data-resilience debates, including at the August 2026 National Geospatial Advisory Committee (NGAC) meeting ("From HIFLD Open to HIFLD Next").
- **Open questions:** Can community-run archives earn users' trust? Will funding and governance last? Do commercial or licensed layers create legal problems if republished?

---

## 10. Key sources

- DHS GMO HIFLD page: dhs.gov/gmo/hifld; 2026 User Forum videos (DHS Media Library)
- 6 U.S.C. § 343; IRTPA § 8201; DHS MD 034-01
- FGDC HIFLD Subcommittee page; 2015 subcommittee minutes; 2018 Nebert Award notice
- NGA press release on the transfer, June 9, 2022
- NAPSG Foundation discontinuation notice and webinar notes
- At These Coordinates (Donnelly), Aug and Dec 2025
- Data Rescue Project posts; DataLumos DOI 10.3886/E241367V1
- source.coop/seerai/hifld; hifld.publicenvirodata.org
- Project Geospatial, "The Phoenix Project"
- geoMusings, "HIFLD Open Is Dead*, Long Live HIFLD" (July 2025)
- My Community Data service audit (March 2026)

# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.

# HIFLD Open: Risk Assessment

## The main finding

HIFLD Open has already been shut down. DHS took the portal offline on **August 26, 2025** and removed the HIFLD website and portal by **September 16, 2025**. Most categories below are therefore scored as having already happened, not as a future risk. The data survives only in non-federal (or DHS-funded academic) archives, frozen as of August 2025. DHS's HIFLD Secure, which only authorized users can access, continues.

## How I scored a portal

HIFLD Open was a portal that gathered and republished about 400 layers made by other agencies. It did not collect data itself. Two things follow:
- **No information collection request (ICR) applies.** HIFLD did not survey the public, so it had no Paperwork Reduction Act approval to expire.
- **I found no Federal Register notice** announcing or explaining the shutdown. DHS announced it through a web page, NAPSG Foundation (a nonprofit partner) notices and webinars.

---

## 1. Historical Data Availability

**Evidence for "Gone"**
- The portal (hifld-geoplatform.hub.arcgis.com / opendata.arcgis.com) and its ArcGIS REST services are offline. The HIFLD website was removed September 16, 2025 (NAPSG notice).
- DHS's "crosswalk" spreadsheet, which linked each layer to its original publisher, was itself taken down in September 2025 (August 2026 FGDC/NGAC presentation, "From HIFLD Open to HIFLD Next").
- NGA (the program's earlier sponsor) removed its own legacy HIFLD services in 2022. No federal copy of the older data remains public.
- The DHS page (dhs.gov/gmo/hifld, last updated September 4, 2025) now describes only HIFLD Secure.

**Evidence for "High Risk" (partial survival)**
- Some layers still exist at the agencies that made them, such as USGS, FEMA and EPA. However, an unverified March 2026 audit by the civic-tech site My Community Data found only about 52 of roughly 365 former service URLs still working.
- Some layers moved only to HIFLD Secure, which the public can't use.

**What still exists outside the primary location**
- DataLumos (run by ICPSR): 415 layers, DOI 10.3886/E241367V1.
- Source Cooperative (SeerAI).
- HIFLD Next (Public Environmental Data Partners).
- Homeland Security Digital Library at the Naval Postgraduate School, which is DHS-funded. Its page says it preserved "an aggregation of those open data sources." I could not open the page itself (403 error).

**Rating: Gone.** Nothing is publicly available at the primary federal location. Copies survive only through third parties.

---

## 2. Future Data Availability

**Evidence for "Gone"**
- DHS ended HIFLD Open, saying it was "no longer a national mission priority."
- Before the shutdown, the notice said "Open datasets are no longer being updated" (quoted on LinkedIn, July 2025).
- No public successor is planned. DHS's 2026 HIFLD User Forum covered only HIFLD Secure, "HIFLD Shared" and the new HIFLD Catalog, all for the homeland security community.

**Other notes:** There is no statutory deadline and no ICR to measure against. Volunteer projects (HIFLD Next and the forming "Commons" coalition) are not federal and don't change this rating.

**Rating: Gone.**

---

## 3. Data Quality

**Evidence for "Gone"**
- Publication has ended. Every surviving copy is frozen at its August 2025 state.
- Archivist Frank Donnelly expects the snapshot to stay current for only "the next couple of years," after which it becomes mainly historical.

**Background issues** (these would have been Moderate or High even before the shutdown)
- Users long complained about outdated records, points with no real location (coordinates 0,0), and missing unique IDs and attributes (HIFLD Next; Nate Smith on LinkedIn, July 2025).
- After the crosswalk vanished, users must pull from many separate sources again, with mixed update schedules.

**Rating: Gone.**

---

## 4. Statutory Context

**Evidence for "High Risk"**
- The law (6 U.S.C. § 343, from IRTPA § 8201) requires DHS to manage geospatial information for critical-infrastructure and emergency missions. It does **not** require a public portal or name specific public datasets.
- Substitute sources exist for many layers, because they came from USGS, FEMA, NOAA, EPA, USACE, Census and Oak Ridge National Laboratory. That made the public aggregation easy to justify cutting.
- DHS policy (Management Directive 034-01) and OMB Circular A-16 set coordination duties, not a duty to publish.

**Evidence for "Moderate Risk"**
- The data clearly supports federal programs, including FEMA, NORTHCOM, the National Interagency Fire Center and fusion centers.
- Some layers produced only by HIFLD have no public substitute.
- But that programmatic use is now met by HIFLD Secure, not the public portal.

**Rating: High Risk.** The authorization is vague about public release, and the shutdown shows it gave no protection.

---

## 5. Staffing and Funding

**Evidence for "High Risk"**
- In April 2025, DHS reportedly planned to cut the **Management Directorate by about 50%**, using deferred resignation, early retirement and layoffs (Federal News Network, April 3, 2025). The Directorate includes the CIO's office, where the Geospatial Management Office (GMO) sits.
- All funding for the public portal itself ended. That would be "Gone" if the scope were only HIFLD Open.

**Evidence for "Moderate Risk"**
- DHS leadership changed: Secretary Noem has since been replaced (the DHS site now lists Secretary Markwayne Mullin).
- Department-wide reorganization and layoffs, including about 1,000 proposed CISA cuts and October 2025 shutdown layoffs (Federal News Network; Nextgov).

**Evidence for "No Known Issue"**
- The FY2026 request for the CIO's office was **$642.4M with 612 positions**, up from $627.9M and 588 positions in FY2025, largely from transfers. The overall Management Directorate request fell only about 1% for appropriated funds (DHS FY26 Congressional Budget Justification).
- GAO found DHS's total workforce fell about **1%** from December 2024 to January 2026, the smallest drop of any major agency.
- GMO still runs HIFLD Secure and holds the annual forum, so the office still exists.

**Gap:** I could not find GMO-specific staffing numbers. The USAJobs tracker page loaded without data and says it will be archived December 31, 2025, so it gave no subagency figures.

**Rating: Moderate Risk.** The office survives and its budget is stable. The threatened 50% cut and the leadership change support Moderate. The termination of the portal itself is better captured under Policy.

---

## 6. Policy

**Evidence for "Gone"**
- DHS ended the public portal in a decision made around March 2025, citing "no longer a national mission priority" (NAPSG; FGDC/NGAC presentation, August 2026).

**Evidence for "High Risk"**
- The change fits Administration priorities. DHS leadership ordered the department "back to its core mission," and DHS Science & Technology was refocused on border, immigration and transnational crime (Nextgov, April 2025).
- The FGDC HIFLD Subcommittee was retired in March 2026.
- DHS gave no cost or security reason, and there was no Federal Register notice or public comment period.

**Rating: Gone.**

---

## What still remains uncertain

- Whether the volunteer archives (HIFLD Next Commons, DataLumos, Source Cooperative) can keep stable funding and governance over time.
- Whether layers held only in HIFLD Secure will ever be made public again.
- Whether source agencies such as FEMA and EPA, themselves facing cuts, will keep publishing the layers the crosswalk pointed to.

---

## Summary of risk levels

- **Historical Data Availability:** Gone
- **Future Data Availability:** Gone
- **Data Quality:** Gone
- **Statutory Context:** High Risk
- **Staffing and Funding:** Moderate Risk
- **Policy:** Gone
